content: Eczema, also known as atopic dermatitis, is a common chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by itchy, red, and dry skin lesions that can vary in severity. It is caused by a combination of genetic, immunologic, and environmental factors that disrupt the skin barrier and immune responses. The condition often begins in childhood but can occur at any age. Eczema is not contagious and frequently coexists with other atopic conditions such as asthma and allergic rhinitis. Key mechanisms include skin barrier dysfunction, immune dysregulation with increased skin inflammation, and heightened sensitivity to environmental triggers like allergens and irritants. Practical management involves skin hydration, avoidance of known triggers, and use of anti-inflammatory medications such as topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors. Lifestyle considerations include identifying and managing stress, maintaining appropriate skin care routines, and dietary evaluation if food sensitivities are suspected. Major synonyms include atopic dermatitis and allergic eczema. Limitations in current understanding include variability in individual response to treatments and challenges in preventing flare-ups. Safety concerns primarily relate to the side effects of long-term topical steroid use and rare systemic medication effects. Comprehensive evaluation and patient-tailored management improve quality of life and reduce complications such as infections. This module provides detailed, evidence-based information to support patient education and inform clinical care.

content: Eczema refers to a group of skin conditions causing inflammation, redness, and itching. The most common form is atopic dermatitis, often simply called eczema. Other types include contact dermatitis, dyshidrotic eczema, nummular eczema, and seborrheic dermatitis. While all involve skin irritation, their causes and clinical features differ. Atopic dermatitis typically affects flexural areas (e.g., inside elbows and behind knees) and is linked to allergy-prone individuals. Recognizing the type of eczema present is essential for targeted management and treatment.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Eczema arises from complex interactions among genetic, environmental, and immunologic factors. A key aspect is the impaired skin barrier due to mutations in the filaggrin gene (FLG), resulting in increased water loss and vulnerability to irritants and allergens. Immune dysregulation with elevated type 2 helper T-cell (Th2) responses promotes inflammation. Environmental triggers such as pollen, dust mites, harsh soaps, and temperature extremes can exacerbate symptoms. Understanding these mechanisms aids in developing personalized treatment plans.

content: Risk factors include family history of eczema, asthma, or hay fever, emphasizing the atopic or allergic predisposition. Early-life exposures such as cesarean delivery, exposure to tobacco smoke, and certain microbial environments also influence risk. Male sex is associated with a slightly higher risk in infancy, but eczema affects all genders. Recognizing risk factors helps identify individuals who may benefit from early interventions.

chunk_title: Symptoms and Clinical Features of Eczema
content: Eczema typically presents with dry, scaly, red patches of skin that itch intensely. In infants, it often affects the face and scalp, while older children and adults experience it in flexural areas. Chronic scratching can cause thickened, leathery skin (lichenification), cracks, and susceptibility to infections. Variability in severity means some may experience mild intermittent flare-ups, while others have persistent, widespread symptoms.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history and physical examination. Criteria include chronic or relapsing dermatitis with characteristic morphology and distribution alongside itchy skin. Additional tests, such as patch testing or skin biopsy, are reserved for differential diagnosis or suspected contact allergens. Severity assessment tools guide treatment intensity. Early and accurate diagnosis ensures appropriate therapeutic strategies and monitoring.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Treatment aims to restore skin barrier function and reduce inflammation. Regular use of emollients/moisturizers is foundational, maintaining hydration and protecting against irritants. Topical corticosteroids are first-line anti-inflammatory agents; potency and duration depend on severity and body site. Calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus) offer steroid-sparing alternatives, especially in sensitive areas. In moderate to severe or refractory cases, phototherapy or systemic immunomodulators like dupilumab may be considered under specialist care. Ongoing research explores emerging biologics targeting immune pathways.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Managing eczema includes identifying and avoiding individual triggers such as allergens, irritants (soaps, detergents), temperature changes, and stress. Maintaining a gentle skin care routine using non-soap cleansers and lukewarm water is beneficial. Clothing made from natural fibers (e.g., cotton) reduces irritation risks. Stress management techniques can contribute to flare-up prevention. Dietary triggers are controversial; some individuals report improvement with elimination diets, but evidence is not robust, warranting individualized approaches.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: A prevalent misconception is that eczema results from poor hygiene or is contagious; in reality, it is an immune-mediated chronic condition not transmitted person-to-person. Another false belief is that topical steroids are unsafe when used appropriately; under medical supervision, they are effective and generally safe. Understanding these misconceptions helps reduce stigma and improve adherence to treatment.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: While topical corticosteroids are effective, prolonged use, especially of high-potency agents, can cause skin thinning, stretch marks, and other side effects. Calcineurin inhibitors carry a black-box warning but are generally safe when used as directed. Phototherapy requires monitoring for skin aging and malignancy risks. Systemic medications necessitate specialist oversight due to potential immune suppression and infection risks. Educating patients on correct use and monitoring helps maximize safety.

content: Untreated or poorly controlled eczema can lead to skin infections (bacterial, viral, fungal), primarily due to scratching and barrier disruption. Chronic inflammation may cause skin thickening and pigment changes. Psychological impacts include sleep disturbances, anxiety, and reduced quality of life. Recognizing complications is critical for timely intervention and multidisciplinary care.

chunk_title: Role of Moisturizers and Emollients in Eczema
content: Emollients and moisturizers are cornerstone therapies for eczema management. They restore the skin barrier by providing hydration and lipids that prevent water loss. Frequent, liberal application reduces itching and inflammation. Various formulations exist, including creams, ointments, and lotions, tailored to patient preference and lesion severity. Consistent use can decrease reliance on anti-inflammatory medications and prevent flare-ups.
